Literature:
Rick Stewart, The American West: Legendary Artists of the Frontier, Dallas, 1986, p. 18; p. 19, illustrated.

Lot Note:
Baltimore painter, Alfred Jacob Miller, produced a compelling visual record of the western fur trade after receiving a significant 1837 commission from Captain William Drummond Stewart, a Scottish patron. Miller traveled with Stewart to the annual fur traders' rendezvous, a vital trade meeting in the Green River Valley of present-day Wyoming. This exchange, facilitated by the American Fur Company, brought together diverse groups, including American mountain men and members of several Native American nations such as the Sioux, Cheyenne, and Crow, allowing them to acquire necessary provisions in exchange for furs. Miller's observational "trail sketches" from the journey became the source material for numerous oil and watercolor paintings, notably a series of 200 oils and watercolors commissioned by William T. Walters in 1858.

These works, delivered with descriptive texts over the next two years, provide not only a detailed visual history but also a window into the prevailing 19th-century biases of the artist and explorer. Miller’s commentary on Schim-a-co-che describes him with equal parts admiration and prejudice, comparing his dignity to that of a "civilized gentleman" while juxtaposing the chief's distinction with "common Indians." The present lot, the creation of which coincides with Miller's output from his travels with Drummond, is part of an invaluable yet historically complex document of this period in the colonization and exploration of the American West.

Lot Note:
According to Scott R. Ferris, Home Again—Asgaard, "depicts Kent's wife Sally and their dog Gunnar greeting [him] on his return home to Asgaard," after what has been, we are led to presume, a lengthy period of travel. Sally running out of the house, her arms raised in apparent excitement, is at the center of the image. Her gaze leads us first to Gunnar and then to the figure of the artist, out of view behind the tree, a hint to his extended absence. The scene, suffused with familial warmth, is indeed a reminder of Kent’s peripatetic life as an artist. To him, exploration and artistic production were inextricable endeavors, and his career took him to remote and rugged regions of the world, which inspired him to distill nature’s harsh and sublime qualities as well as humanity’s loneliness and resilience. By contrast, his house in Asgaard, which he called Gladsheim, provided an anchor of safety and comfort in a bucolic setting. Sadly, Ferris continues, the dwelling "was destroyed by fire in 1969," but Kent quickly "redesigned and built their new home on the same foundation."

Lot Note:
The paintings that Milton Avery produced in the Gaspé Bay are rare. Oxcart is no exception, having sold directly from the artist’s studio in May 1940 to The Valentine Gallery in New York.

The Gaspé landscapes are significant as they represent a critical moment in the artist’s career, when Avery began to use color as his primary means of expression. Its structural function is reflected in the restricted, darker palette in the foreground, in which Avery channels the art of Pablo Picasso and George Braque to set the emotional tone of the scene–a difficult act of labor under the beating summer sun. In contrast, the sky and sea are set in striking blue and green tones, which elevate the overall composition and give it a sense of reverie and quietude.

Following in the Cubists’ footsteps, Avery reinterprets a traditional pastoral scene as a two-dimensional arrangement of forms, tones, and textures–all simplified. The slightly skewed perspective reinforces the flatness of the pictorial space, allowing Avery to achieve his signature synthesis between realism and abstraction, making Oxcart a quintessential piece of his 1940s production.

Above all, the work reflects Avery’s attachment to the landscape, specifically the New England seaside along Gloucester, a place he first visited in 1920 and often returned to between then and 1945 with his wife Sally. The sea held a profound meaning for Avery throughout his life. "We were followers of the sea,” Sally Avery reminisced. “On the beaches of Provincetown, Gloucester and Gaspé we braved the surf and rocky shore, spending endless hours contemplating the sea...Always the sea beckoned, at times with figures, at times with boats. But it was the sea, alternately black and mysterious or ruddy and gay that expressed the mystery and independence that makes its lure unfathomable. For Milton this was a subject to challenge again and again.” Here, the emerald-green sea occupies much of the composition. It enlivens it and acts as a literal pool of reflection and contemplation; it hints at a metaphorical space beyond, which contrasts with the prosaic scene in the foreground.

Lot Note:
In A Winter Panorama, Nunamaker exploits a horizontal canvas of 42 inches to emphasize the beauty–and sheer breadth–of Bucks County, Pennsylvania. He anchors the composition with the textural weight of a stone farmhouse at left, which serves as a foil to the snow-covered hills on the horizon. The near-monochromatic foreground trees stand starkly against a sky that is both heavily laden with leaden gray clouds and fractured by patches of vibrant cerulean. This light transforms the snow, which is rendered not in pure white, but with subtle gradations of blue, demonstrating Nunamaker's mastery of the optical effects of winter air and his sensitivity to a resonant regional realism that captures the occasionally severe, yet compelling beauty of the Bucks County landscape.

Lot Note:
Shad Fisherman No. 2 exemplifies a key moment in John Fulton Folinsbee’s transition from Impressionism toward a bolder, more uninhibited strain of Modernism. While firmly rooted in the observed reality of riverside labor in his beloved Pennsylvania, the painting transcends pure representation to achieve what Folinsbee increasingly sought in his mature work: a synthesis of modernist execution with Impressionist sensitivity conveyed through atmosphere, color, and the interplay of light. Indeed, and as Kirsten Jensen aptly observes, “the real subjects of Shad Fisherman No. 2 are light—the stark contrasts between the looming clouds and the summer sky—and the moody anticipation of the storm to come."

The fishermen, quickly sketched in a strokes, were among Folinsbee's favorite subjects. Although they add a bit of human activity, here they merely serve as a means to cast the various effects of the light, some blinding white while others blend with the blue-shadowed casting net, thus heightening the drama of the coming storm. Here, Folinsbee departs from the more linear construction of his earlier industrial landscapes, which marked his first attempts at Modernism, and instead orchestrates a swirling vortex of movement, using sweeping brushwork and intensified tonal contrasts to accentuate the dramatic effect of the moment, thus underscoring the emotional power of what appears to be, at first glance, a very mundane activity.

Shad Fisherman No. 2 is emblematic of Folinsbee’s finest works from the late 1930s in that it embodies the artist’s deepening engagement with Modernist ideas, particularly the atmospheric mysticism championed by Arthur Bowen Davies, whom Folinsbee deeply admired (alongside Robert Henri), and whose landscapes Duncan Phillips praised for their affinities with Cézanne and El Greco. The darkened palette, heightened shadow-play, and compressed composition in the present work all reflect this influence, transforming the scene of shad fishing into an eternal, almost mythical American life tableau, which would led contemporary art critic Edward Alden Jewell to hail Folinsbee as “one of the lords of impasto, who can swing his brush with an authority that is boisterous but that seldom falls short of capturing the effect desired.”

Lot Note:
Born in Summit, New Jersey in 1876 and trained at Columbia University’s School of Architecture, Colt initially joined a New York architectural firm before abandoning the discipline altogether, eager to escape what he once described as the restrictive demands of “clients’ tastes or whimsies.” Drawn instead to the freedom of artistic expression, Colt settled at Phillips’ Mill, where he formed a close friendship with William Langson Lathrop, Edward Willis Redfield, Daniel Garber, Charles Rosen, Rae Sloan Bredin, and Robert Spencer–the first generation of New Hope School painters. Though he pursued painting, design, and crafts with equal devotion, Colt is remembered today primarily for his luminous Impressionist landscapes, which he composed in the studio because of a chronic heart condition that prevented prolonged outdoor study.

The present painting stands apart within the limited corpus of Colt’s work. The largest known oil by the artist, it represents one of his most ambitious surviving compositions ever to appear on the market. On the monumental canvas, Colt inscribes a now-vanished chapter of life along the Delaware River with an almost cinematic immediacy. Rather than offering a distant vista, Colt brings the viewer directly onto the river, where the diagonal movement of a barge contrasts gently with the horizontal (and echoing) banks as well as the rustling canopy of trees overhead. A figure stands at the stern, pole in hand, while a team of mules waits at the riverbank; small yet evocative details that anchor the composition in lived history. In this sentimental view, Colt memorializes the everyday labor and quiet poetry of river life before mechanization transformed the region’s rhythms forever.

Colt’s brisk, shimmering brushstrokes animate the reflections on the river’s surface, while the bright, sun-filled palette envelops the entire composition in a sense of warmth and pastoral calm. The canvas resonates with nostalgia, not only because it preserves a nearly forgotten mode of transportation, but because Colt renders it through a screen of dappled light, mirrored water and soft atmospheric haze, which transforms the industrial subject into an homage to the enduring beauty of Bucks County.

Colt died suddenly of a heart attack in 1926, leaving many canvases unfinished and an even greater number tragically destroyed by subsequent occupants of his home. This historic loss makes the reappearance of the present canvas on the market even more exciting and momentous.

Lot Note:
Daniel Garber’s career as a painter can be distilled as a heartfelt celebration of Bucks County—of its hilly topography, humbly quaint architecture, and slow-paced rural lifestyle. The tight composition of Solebury–Springtime, centered on the stone buildings surrounded by burgeoning trees and deep green grass, conveys the close bond between man and nature, the fact that, in Bucks County, life is inextricably tied to the land.

Garber emphasizes natural simplicity as the source of bliss, eschewing the rapid changes brought about by urbanization and industrialization. The scene is bathed in warm sunlight, the nascent springtime evoking rebirth and even the perpetuation of a flourishing way of life established from time immemorial. The motif of the sheep in the foreground and the raw stone of the barn on the left further the notion that simplicity is indeed the antidote to a tiresome and overwrought lifestyle.

But Garber’s celebration of simplicity is not limited to symbolism. His painting, in a very formal dimension, is in fact a feat of artistry, at once concealing and illuminating artifice, only to make his point about simplicity even starker. The three figures, immersed in both scenery and conversation, appear completely oblivious to the viewer, and by extension, to the fact that they are objects of contemplation, just like the artwork they inhabit. Here, Garber acknowledges his craft, the inherently designed nature of his landscape, while simultaneously suggesting that it is not exactly what is worthy of our attention. Instead, what we are compelled to recognize is the simple, authentic, idyllic—devoid of unnecessary artifice—quality of the place that the three figures also embrace and embody.
